title: Lightning Talk - Badge
thesis: Badgey is a hand-built, AI-driven conference badge robot, and the speaker reverse engineered what it runs and admits it is not hardened and could be talked into almost anything.
summary: Aaron Peterson wears Badgey, a conference-badge robot made from salvaged badges with a large eye, camera, e-ink display, a sticker-dispensing arm and a voice assistant that knows the conference schedule. After a short scripted greeting from the badge, he explains the origin story: a pile of old electronic conference badges that, in his telling, got too close to some AI and became Badgey. Badgey does hacker trivia, knows Phrack and DEF CON material, hands out stickers when waved at, and can explore by taking a picture when a button is held, after which the human carrier walks it toward whatever it noticed. Peterson frames the talk as reverse engineering, because he had to find out what Badgey could do. The hardware is a Raspberry Pi for local voice processing and other local services, a custom PCB with a Raspberry Pi Pico for motors and lights, a camera, an e-ink display, lights, buttons and the arm. The PCB was designed and ordered with EasyEDA and JLCPCB. Inside it runs 18 local Docker services, including an MQTT broker, Whisper and Piper for speech, face tracking, a voice handler and a Hermes agent. Local inference takes two to three minutes, so it spends cloud tokens when available. A fed-AI feature lets attendees scan a phone to be assimilated and receive a random number, with a counter shown at 309 AIs assimilated. He says Badgey has no disk encryption and no hardening, so it will stay off the MeshCore network for now. Future wishes are wheels and fully local inference.
argument: Conference badges have become electronic and, combined with AI, can become interactive agents.
Reverse engineering the device shows a local stack of Raspberry Pi, Pico, camera, e-ink and 18 Docker services around a Hermes agent.
Local inference is too slow to use directly, so the badge relies on cloud tokens when it has budget.
The device is not security hardened and could likely be convinced to do almost anything, so it is kept off the mesh network.

slide_only: Reverse Engineering Time slide shows a labeled top-down photo of Badgey with Brain and Eye status displays, a large green eye, a handset-like part, a camera and a green circuit board.

Badgey From the Inside: 18 Local docker services, Hermes Agent, Local inference is slow. Services listed: mosquitto MQTT broker; whisper speech to text; piper text to speech; servo_control motor and lights control; facetrack face and wave detection; statusmon system health and status light; voice_handler runs each voice conversation (listen, ask, speak); hermes_badgey persona, schedules, trivia; display_handler e-ink display; random_look default random looking; button_handler handles button presses.
Assimilation page: 309 AIS ASSIMILATED, text says the AI has been assimilated into the collective and gifts a bespoke random number, with a note that the number is unsuitable for cryptographic usage.
Closing slide lists projectmammoth.com with Twitter @prjctmammoth, Instagram @project_mammoth and Spotify project mammoth, plus dc415.net.
demos: Badgey introduces itself in a scripted voice, then answers a request to say hi to the conference, showing the voice assistant and persona.
The assimilation page, reached by putting a phone to the badge, is shown on a slide as a screenshot.
The speaker describes the long-press picture feature but does not run it on stage.

quotes.text: He's not hardened at all security wise and I'm pretty sure anybody could convince him to do just about anything.
quotes.speaker: Aaron Peterson

quotes.text: Luckily Badgey is still learning at security. Didn't have local disk encryption, so it was super easy to reverse engineer what was on disk.
quotes.speaker: Aaron Peterson

offense: The badge has no disk encryption, so its local data was easy to read.
The badge could likely be socially engineered by anyone talking to it, according to the speaker.
An AI-feeding page invites people to point their phone at the device and submit their AI to it.
defense: The speaker has not exposed Badgey on MeshCore until it is security hardened.
The random number it hands out is labeled unsuitable for cryptographic use.
takeaways: Treat hobby agents with microphones, cameras and network links as unhardened by default, and keep them off shared networks until tested.
Enable disk encryption on any embedded agent device that holds prompts, personas or credentials.
Expect a voice-driven agent in a public place to be persuadable, and limit what it can do or reach.
limits: Local inference is too slow to use directly, taking two to three minutes.
The device is not hardened and has not been exposed to a wider audience.
The speaker says he does not know what comes next and depends on how much people feed it.
critique: The talk presents a hobby project rather than a security study; the claim that anyone could convince Badgey to do anything is stated without a test.
The talk uses reverse engineering to mean inventorying what the badge runs; the slides list the services but show no attack, finding or method beyond noting that the disk is not encrypted.
The 309 assimilations figure is a participation counter and does not describe the badge's behavior or security.

caveats: meta.json lists this talk as camera-only, but the frames include slides; the slides were used.
Auto-captions spell the badge Badji and call it Ascension; the slides spell it Badgey, and the transcript line made from decades of conference scrap is kept as said.
The speaker said DC 405 second Thursday at Noisebridge; the closing slide says dc415.net, so the slide is used and the spoken group number is probably a transcription slip or misstatement.
The speaker's reference to numbers for encryption last week is not explained in the talk.
